cycles_and_structure.title: Bull & Bear Markets
cycles_and_structure.subtitle: What separates a sustained rally from a sustained decline.
cycles_and_structure.what_this_is: A bull market is a sustained period of rising prices, typically defined as a 20% or more gain from a recent low. A bear market is the reverse — a 20% or more decline from a recent high. These aren't precise thresholds set by any official body; they're conventions the market adopted to describe large, directional moves that persist across weeks or months. The defining feature isn't the percentage — it's the duration and the shift in underlying conditions.
cycles_and_structure.key_ideas:
1. The 20% threshold is a convention, not a law — markets don't know they're in a bear market at −19.9%.
2. Bull markets historically last longer than bear markets. Bear markets tend to be sharper and faster.
3. Sectors rotate differently within each regime: defensives outperform in bears, cyclicals in early bulls.
4. Sentiment often lags price. Bear markets often end before the headlines change.
5. Sharp rallies inside bear markets (bear-market rallies) can be indistinguishable from reversals in real time.
cycles_and_structure.in_market_pulse: Market Posture tracks the broad regime read — expanding, contracting, or transitional. Tactical Momentum's VIX and Fear & Greed gauges, and Systemic Risk's credit spread gauge, capture the stress level within a regime. The Overview digest contextualises these in the day's market narrative. These describe the current configuration, not the next one.
cycles_and_structure.doesnt_tell_you: The app's regime read reflects current conditions, not predictions of when the regime changes. Bear markets end before most indicators confirm it — the turn is only visible in hindsight. No signal in this app identifies a regime change in real time.

cycles_and_structure.title: Market Tops
cycles_and_structure.subtitle: How a bull market usually ends before the decline begins.
cycles_and_structure.what_this_is: A market top is the price level at which a bull market ends before a sustained decline begins. Tops are rarely single-day events — they're typically processes: distribution phases where selling gradually overtakes buying, sometimes over weeks or months, while prices drift sideways or make smaller, less convincing new highs. The process is often only recognisable once the decline is well underway.
cycles_and_structure.key_ideas:
1. Volume often diverges from price at tops — new highs on declining volume can signal weakening conviction.
2. Breadth narrows: the index may still be rising, but fewer stocks are participating.
3. Sentiment extremes (low VIX, high bullish sentiment) are often present at tops but can persist longer than expected.
4. Leadership rotates toward defensives before the index confirms a downtrend.
5. Internal deterioration — breadth, volume, sector rotation — often precedes the price peak.
cycles_and_structure.in_market_pulse: Tactical Momentum tracks sentiment extremes through Fear & Greed, Put/Call, and VIX. Systemic Risk's market breadth gauge watches participation directly — how many stocks are confirming the index move. Market Posture labels the current regime. Collectively, these can show when conditions resemble a late-cycle distribution phase — but the app names what's present, not what comes next.
cycles_and_structure.doesnt_tell_you: No indicator reliably identifies a top in real time. Many conditions that resemble a top resolve without one — sometimes multiple times before a top actually forms. The app does not forecast turning points.

cycles_and_structure.title: Market Bottoms & Capitulation
cycles_and_structure.subtitle: The selling climax that often marks where a bear market ends.
cycles_and_structure.what_this_is: A market bottom is the price level at which a bear market ends before a sustained recovery begins. Capitulation is the phase just before a bottom — where selling accelerates sharply, driven by forced liquidation, margin calls, or exhaustion. It creates a final, often violent decline that clears the sellers. Bottoms tend to be faster and more chaotic than tops.
cycles_and_structure.key_ideas:
1. Capitulation is characterised by high volume, sharp intraday moves, and extreme sentiment readings.
2. Fear & Greed and VIX often spike sharply at or near bottoms.
3. Breadth collapses broadly — most things selling down together simultaneously.
4. The first bounce off a bottom is often sharp but not always the start of a new bull market.
5. Bear market lows are confirmed only after sustained recovery, not at the moment of the low.
cycles_and_structure.in_market_pulse: Tactical Momentum's VIX and Fear & Greed gauges measure the sentiment and volatility stress present in the market now. Systemic Risk's credit spread gauge shows whether that stress is showing up in credit markets too. Extreme readings — a VIX spike, Fear & Greed at extreme fear, spreads sharply wide — can reflect capitulation-like conditions. Market Posture tracks whether conditions are contracting or beginning to stabilise.
cycles_and_structure.doesnt_tell_you: Extreme fear readings don't mark bottoms — they mark fear. The same conditions can occur at −20% or −50% into a decline. The app measures the stress level, not when the stress resolves.

cycles_and_structure.title: Market Phases
cycles_and_structure.subtitle: The recurring stages markets move through — recovery, expansion, distribution, decline.
cycles_and_structure.what_this_is: Markets move through recognisable phases: early recovery (accumulation), expansion (markup), late cycle (distribution), and decline (markdown). These aren't perfectly sequential — they overlap, some phases repeat or extend, and the labels are easier to apply in retrospect than in real time. Understanding the phase helps explain why certain sectors and signals are behaving the way they are.
cycles_and_structure.key_ideas:
1. Early recovery: breadth improving, defensive sectors giving way to cyclicals, credit stress fading.
2. Expansion: broad participation, momentum dominant, sentiment rising, new highs across sectors.
3. Late cycle: narrowing leadership, valuations stretched, volatility picking up, early defensive rotation.
4. Decline: breadth collapsing, credit stress rising, defensive outperformance, fear-extreme sentiment.
5. Phases don't have fixed durations, and markets can cycle through sub-phases within each.
cycles_and_structure.in_market_pulse: Market Posture assigns an overall expansion/contraction/transitional label. Market Positioning tracks sector rotation — which sectors lead and which lag. Systemic Risk's market breadth gauge captures the participation signature associated with each phase. Together these describe the signal configuration associated with a phase, not a named phase label.
cycles_and_structure.doesnt_tell_you: Phase labels are interpretive frames, not clockwork. The app reflects the current signal configuration — not a phase forecast or a duration estimate. Markets can stay in a phase configuration far longer than any signal suggests they should.

sentiment_and_behaviour.title: Contrarian Investing Basics
sentiment_and_behaviour.subtitle: Betting against the crowd when consensus has likely overshot reality.
sentiment_and_behaviour.what_this_is: Contrarian investing is an approach built on the premise that market consensus — reflected in price, positioning, and sentiment — can overshoot reality in both directions. When most participants are positioned the same way and expect the same outcome, the conditions exist for that consensus to be wrong. A contrarian read looks for where positioning and sentiment have diverged from what fundamentals would support, or where extremes in one direction have accumulated.
sentiment_and_behaviour.key_ideas:
1. Extreme bullish sentiment (near-universal optimism) often precedes reversals — but timing is uncertain.
2. Put/Call ratios measure options positioning: very low ratios reflect complacency; very high signal fear.
3. NAAIM exposure tracks active-manager equity positioning — extremes in either direction are meaningful.
4. The "pain trade" is the one that moves against the majority position and catches the consensus offside.
5. Contrarian signals require a catalyst to resolve — they can persist a long time without one.
sentiment_and_behaviour.in_market_pulse: Tactical Momentum's Put/Call and Fear & Greed gauges, and the NAAIM exposure gauge within Posture, all measure where participants are positioned and how they feel. Extreme readings describe where consensus sits and where it's most crowded — the precondition for a contrarian outcome, not a prediction of one.
sentiment_and_behaviour.doesnt_tell_you: Sentiment extremes are necessary but not sufficient for reversals. The app measures where consensus sits. When the consensus breaks — and what breaks it — is not determinable from sentiment data alone.

sentiment_and_behaviour.title: The Role of Liquidity
sentiment_and_behaviour.subtitle: How much cash and credit is sloshing around — and why it moves every asset at once.
sentiment_and_behaviour.what_this_is: Liquidity has two distinct meanings in markets. Market liquidity describes how easily an asset can be bought or sold without significantly moving its price. Monetary liquidity describes how much cash and credit is available in the financial system broadly. Monetary liquidity — driven by Federal Reserve policy, bank lending conditions, and market functioning — is one of the most powerful forces shaping risk appetite across all asset classes simultaneously.
sentiment_and_behaviour.key_ideas:
1. When monetary conditions are loose (low rates, ample credit), risk assets tend to benefit as capital seeks return.
2. When conditions tighten (rising rates, credit contraction), risk appetite typically contracts across the board.
3. Market liquidity deteriorates in stress: bid-ask spreads widen, depth thins, and price moves become larger.
4. Credit spreads — high-yield corporate bonds vs. Treasuries — are a widely-used proxy for market-wide risk liquidity.
5. Liquidity crises — where the market mechanism itself seizes — are rare but create severe, fast dislocations.
sentiment_and_behaviour.in_market_pulse: Systemic Risk's credit spread gauge (high-yield corporate bonds vs. Treasuries) reflects risk-liquidity conditions. Widening spreads signal stress; tightening signals easing risk appetite. Macro Vitals' Treasury yield gauge reflects where rates sit, and Systemic Risk's yield curve gauge reflects how the curve is shaped — together these frame the monetary liquidity backdrop.
sentiment_and_behaviour.doesnt_tell_you: The app shows current liquidity conditions. Liquidity can shift quickly and without warning — a single Fed communication, a credit event, or a forced-selling episode can change conditions within hours. The app reflects what's measured now.

sentiment_and_behaviour.title: Sentiment & Positioning
sentiment_and_behaviour.subtitle: Fear, greed, and crowd positioning, and where the app actually tracks them.
sentiment_and_behaviour.what_this_is: Markets move on more than fundamentals — how investors feel about risk shifts prices too, sometimes faster than the underlying data changes. A handful of indicators try to measure that feeling directly, mostly by looking at what investors are actually doing with their money rather than what they say.
sentiment_and_behaviour.key_ideas:
1. Fear & Greed and the Put/Call ratio (CNN): gauge short-term market mood. Extreme fear has historically coincided with periods where selling pressure was overdone, extreme greed with periods of elevated risk-taking — neither is a timing signal on its own, and both can stay at an extreme for a long time.
2. NAAIM Exposure Index: tracks how invested active fund managers actually are, week to week — a direct measure of professional positioning rather than a survey response.
3. AAII Sentiment Survey: measures individual investor sentiment (bullish/neutral/bearish) — a widely watched but famously unreliable contrarian indicator. Extreme readings in either direction are sometimes read as a sign a consensus view has gotten crowded, not as confirmation the consensus is right.
4. CFTC Commitment of Traders (COT) report and FINRA short interest data: show what large futures traders and short sellers are positioned for — institutional-level positioning that moves on a different timescale than retail sentiment.
sentiment_and_behaviour.in_market_pulse: This family appears in Tactical Momentum (Fear & Greed, Put/Call) and in the Posture and Positioning gauges. Posture combines NAAIM, SqueezeMetrics' Dark Index (DIX), and net liquidity signals; Positioning combines AAII, COT futures data, and FINRA short interest. Each is one input among several — none is used alone anywhere in the app.
sentiment_and_behaviour.doesnt_tell_you: None of these measures predict when a crowded position unwinds, or what triggers it. A sentiment extreme can persist for months before anything changes, and two of the crowds tracked here (COT, FINRA short interest) report on a lag of days to weeks — by the time a reading appears, positioning may have already shifted.

valuation_and_rates.title: P/E Expansion & Contraction Cycle
valuation_and_rates.subtitle: Why prices can rise or fall without earnings changing at all.
valuation_and_rates.what_this_is: A stock's price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio reflects how much investors are willing to pay for each dollar of earnings. When that willingness grows — usually when rates are low, growth expectations are rising, or sentiment is positive — the P/E expands, and prices rise even without earnings growth. When willingness shrinks, prices can fall even if earnings hold. The P/E cycle often runs independently of the earnings cycle, driven largely by interest rates and risk appetite.
valuation_and_rates.key_ideas:
1. Low interest rates support higher P/E: future earnings are worth more when discounted at a lower rate.
2. Rising rates compress P/E: the same future earnings are worth less at higher discount rates.
3. Sector-relative P/E reveals where within the market the expansion or compression is occurring.
4. P/E is as much a sentiment measure as a fundamental one — it can overshoot in either direction.
5. Earnings growth can "grow into" a high P/E over time, or earnings disappointment can make a low P/E look worse.
valuation_and_rates.in_market_pulse: Valuation's P/E gauge tracks the S&P 500's trailing P/E against its own historical range — cheap, fair value, or expensive relative to where it's traded before. On an individual stock's fundamentals, the sector-relative P/E metric measures that stock's own P/E against its sector's median, controlling for the fact that some sectors structurally trade richer than others. Macro Vitals' Treasury yield gauge provides the rate context that drives the expansion/compression backdrop.
valuation_and_rates.doesnt_tell_you: P/E ratios don't forecast earnings. High P/E can stay high; low P/E can go lower. The app's valuation read reflects current pricing relative to history — not a directional signal about where prices go from here.

valuation_and_rates.title: Growth vs. Value
valuation_and_rates.subtitle: Two investing styles that trade leadership as rates rise and fall.
valuation_and_rates.what_this_is: Growth stocks are priced for future earnings growth — investors pay a premium today for what they expect the company to earn tomorrow. Value stocks are priced cheaply relative to current earnings, book value, or cash flow — investors pay less, often because growth is slower or the business is temporarily out of favour. The rotation between these two styles is one of the most persistent patterns in equity markets, and it's strongly tied to where interest rates are and where they're heading.
valuation_and_rates.key_ideas:
1. Growth outperforms when rates are low or falling — high-growth future earnings discount more favourably at lower rates.
2. Value tends to outperform when rates are rising or the economy is accelerating — current earnings matter more.
3. The gap between growth and value can persist for years before rotating — both trends run longer than intuition suggests.
4. Tech and consumer discretionary are typically growth-heavy sectors; financials, energy, and utilities are typically value-heavy.
5. Relative performance between sectors reflects style rotation even without an explicit growth/value label.
valuation_and_rates.in_market_pulse: Market Positioning's sector rotation tracks which sectors are leading or lagging the broader market — when growth-heavy sectors like technology and consumer discretionary lead while value-heavy sectors like financials lag, that reflects a growth-leading configuration, and vice versa. On individual stocks, the sector-relative P/E metric on the fundamentals section shows whether a specific stock is priced richly or cheaply against its own sector. Macro Vitals' rate context frames the driver behind any rotation.
valuation_and_rates.doesnt_tell_you: The app doesn't label a "growth regime" or "value regime." The sector rotation pattern describes the current configuration; whether rates and growth expectations support the current spread — and when that changes — requires judgement beyond the gauges.

valuation_and_rates.title: Fed Policy Cycles
valuation_and_rates.subtitle: How the Fed's rate decisions ripple through the entire market backdrop.
valuation_and_rates.what_this_is: The Federal Reserve uses its benchmark interest rate (the Federal Funds Rate) to manage inflation and employment — its dual mandate. When inflation is high, the Fed raises rates to slow the economy and reduce price pressure. When growth slows or employment weakens, it cuts rates to stimulate activity. These tightening and easing cycles shape the entire financial market backdrop: cost of capital, risk appetite, currency values, credit conditions, and asset pricing all respond.
valuation_and_rates.key_ideas:
1. Rate hike cycles typically compress P/E and pressure growth stocks, high-yield credit, and speculative assets.
2. Rate cut cycles tend to support risk assets: cheaper financing, higher present value of future earnings.
3. The yield curve shape (short vs. long rates) reflects market expectations of future Fed action.
4. Inverted yield curves — where short rates exceed long rates — have historically preceded recessions, with a variable and sometimes lengthy lag.
5. Markets begin pricing rate changes well before they occur; futures markets reflect evolving Fed expectations continuously.
valuation_and_rates.in_market_pulse: Macro Vitals tracks the Fed funds rate and the 10-year Treasury yield. Systemic Risk's yield curve gauge tracks the spread between short and long rates. The diagram below illustrates how normal, flat, and inverted curves compare. Together these reflect where the current cycle sits — tightening, paused, or easing — based on current rate levels and curve configuration.
valuation_and_rates.doesnt_tell_you: The app reflects current rate levels and curve shape. Fed policy decisions are not predictable from these signals alone — and market pricing of future cuts or hikes changes continuously and is frequently revised. The app shows what the market currently prices in; whether that's correct is not answerable here.

valuation_and_rates.title: Valuation Basics
valuation_and_rates.subtitle: Whether a stock's price is reasonable relative to what it actually earns.
valuation_and_rates.what_this_is: Valuation asks a different question than sentiment or technicals: is the price being paid reasonable relative to what the company actually earns? The P/E ratio (price divided by earnings per share) is the most common starting point — a "high" P/E means the market is paying more per dollar of current earnings, often because it expects faster future growth; a "low" P/E can mean the opposite, or that the market has real concerns the price hasn't priced out.
valuation_and_rates.key_ideas:
1. Sector-relative P/E: comparing a stock's P/E to its own sector, rather than to the market as a whole, controls for the fact that some industries structurally trade at higher multiples than others (growth software vs. utilities, for example) — a stock that looks "cheap" against the whole market can be expensive against its actual peers, and vice versa.
2. Low valuation isn't automatically a bargain: it's frequently a sign the market has already priced in a real risk. Valuation is one lens among several, not a standalone verdict.
valuation_and_rates.in_market_pulse: This is the sector-relative P/E metric on each stock's fundamentals — the stock's own P/E measured against its sector's median, computed from the same underlying data as the headline P/E figure, not a separate estimate.
valuation_and_rates.doesnt_tell_you: A P/E ratio doesn't say why it's high or low. A cheap stock can stay cheap for a reason the market has already priced in, and an expensive one can keep re-rating higher. Valuation is a starting question, not an answer on its own.

risk_and_price_action.title: Volatility Regimes
risk_and_price_action.subtitle: Calm markets and choppy ones, and how VIX tells them apart.
risk_and_price_action.what_this_is: Volatility measures how much prices move over a given period. A low-volatility regime is characterised by small daily moves, tight bid-ask spreads, and broadly calm investor behaviour. A high-volatility regime features large daily swings, wider spreads, and elevated risk perception. VIX — the CBOE Volatility Index — measures the 30-day implied volatility on S&P 500 options contracts and is the most widely-followed proxy for market-wide volatility expectations.
risk_and_price_action.key_ideas:
1. VIX below 20 is historically associated with calm, compressed, or range-bound market conditions.
2. VIX between 20 and 29 reflects elevated, choppier-than-usual conditions; 30 or above is a panic-level extreme-fear reading.
3. Volatility tends to cluster — high-volatility periods follow high-volatility periods rather than alternating with calm.
4. VIX and S&P 500 prices are typically inversely correlated: spikes in VIX often accompany sharp index declines.
5. Sustained low VIX can precede reversals — complacency builds risk, not safety.
risk_and_price_action.in_market_pulse: Tactical Momentum includes VIX as a primary gauge, alongside Fear & Greed and Put/Call. The app tracks VIX level and whether it sits in calm, elevated, or panic territory relative to historical norms. Fear & Greed provides a composite sentiment read that incorporates volatility alongside other measures.
risk_and_price_action.doesnt_tell_you: VIX measures options pricing — what the options market implies about future volatility, not what volatility will actually be. The app shows where VIX sits relative to its own history. The app does not use VIX to predict directional market moves; its primary role here is as a stress indicator, not a price signal.

risk_and_price_action.title: Relative Strength
risk_and_price_action.subtitle: Whether a stock or sector is outperforming its benchmark, even if its price is falling.
risk_and_price_action.what_this_is: Relative strength measures how a stock or sector is performing compared to a benchmark — usually the S&P 500. A stock with rising relative strength is outperforming; falling relative strength means underperforming, even if the absolute price is rising. Relative strength is not the RSI (Relative Strength Index), which is a momentum oscillator using a single price series. Relative strength is a direct ratio comparison of one price series to another.
risk_and_price_action.key_ideas:
1. Sector relative strength rotation is one of the most consistent features of market cycles.
2. Defensives (utilities, healthcare, consumer staples) typically outperform in late-cycle and bear markets.
3. Cyclicals (technology, consumer discretionary, industrials) typically outperform in early-cycle and expansion.
4. A stock making new highs while the broader index doesn't signals strong relative strength — a potential leadership indicator.
5. Relative strength is a comparison, not a level — a stock can have strong relative strength while its price falls.
risk_and_price_action.in_market_pulse: Market Positioning captures sector rotation — which sectors are leading or lagging the broader market. This is the closest equivalent to a relative-strength read within the app, applied at the sector level rather than to individual stocks.
risk_and_price_action.doesnt_tell_you: The app's sector positioning read is based on the engine's inputs and interpretation, not a direct live price-ratio comparison. Individual stock relative strength is not computed or displayed. This article describes how relative strength works as a concept; the app applies it at sector resolution only.

risk_and_price_action.title: Correlation Breakdown in Stress
risk_and_price_action.subtitle: Why diversification can disappear exactly when stress hits hardest.
risk_and_price_action.what_this_is: In normal market conditions, different assets have different, relatively stable correlations to each other — stocks and bonds may move in opposite directions; sectors diverge based on their economic sensitivity. In stress events, correlations converge: almost everything falls together, almost at once. Forced selling — driven by margin calls, fund redemptions, or a flight to safety — affects assets simultaneously regardless of their underlying fundamentals. The diversification that worked in normal conditions appears to collapse precisely when it's needed most.
risk_and_price_action.key_ideas:
1. Forced selling drives correlated drawdowns across asset classes that normally move independently.
2. Short-term Treasuries and gold are among the few assets that reliably hold or appreciate in severe stress events.
3. Credit spreads typically widen sharply in correlation-breakdown events and often lead the equity decline.
4. Sector diversification inside equities offers much less protection than cross-asset diversification in severe stress.
5. Correlations typically normalise after stress resolves, but the timing of normalisation is unpredictable.
risk_and_price_action.in_market_pulse: Systemic Risk's credit spread gauge, and Tactical Momentum's VIX and Fear & Greed gauges, capture the stress indicators that historically precede or accompany correlation breakdown. When multiple gauges across both domains spike simultaneously, that configuration describes elevated systemic stress. Market Posture's contraction label reflects the broad regime consequence.
risk_and_price_action.doesnt_tell_you: The app shows whether systemic stress signals are elevated now. Correlation-breakdown events are unpredictable in timing and severity. The app does not distinguish between a temporary risk-off episode and a systemic liquidity crisis — both look similar in early signal, and only the resolution reveals which it was. This article describes a dynamic that can be partially observed in the Systemic Risk domain but cannot be predicted or forecast from within the app.

market_fundamentals.title: Macro & Interest Rates
market_fundamentals.subtitle: How interest rates set the cost of money for everything else.
market_fundamentals.what_this_is: Interest rates set the "cost of money" for the entire economy, so changes to them ripple into nearly everything else. When the Federal Reserve raises rates, borrowing gets more expensive for companies and consumers alike — which can slow spending and earnings growth, and tends to make already-established cash flows (like bonds, or stocks priced heavily on future growth) relatively more attractive than before. Rate cuts generally work in the opposite direction. Neither effect is instant or guaranteed — markets often move on the expectation of a rate change well before the change itself happens.
market_fundamentals.key_ideas:
1. 10-year and 2-year Treasury yields: the spread between them is widely watched because an inverted yield curve (short-term yields above long-term) has historically preceded economic slowdowns — though the timing and reliability of that relationship varies a lot across cycles.
2. Inflation data (CPI, core PCE): a primary input into what the Fed does next — hotter-than-expected readings tend to raise the odds of tighter policy, and vice versa.
market_fundamentals.in_market_pulse: This appears in Macro Vitals (the Fed funds rate, the 10-year yield, CPI and core PCE inflation, unemployment) and, for the yield curve, in Systemic Risk — all built from FRED data, the same source the Fed itself publishes.
market_fundamentals.doesnt_tell_you: The lag between a rate move — or an inverted curve — and its effect on the economy is long and variable, sometimes over a year, never the same length twice. The app shows where rates and inflation stand today; it doesn't predict the Fed's next move or how long any effect takes to show up.

market_fundamentals.title: Technical Concepts
market_fundamentals.subtitle: Reading price and volume patterns as a reflection of what the market believes.
market_fundamentals.what_this_is: Technical analysis looks at price and volume patterns themselves, on the theory that price action reflects everything the market currently knows or believes, even before that shows up elsewhere.
market_fundamentals.key_ideas:
1. Moving averages: smooth out day-to-day noise to show the underlying trend — the 50-day and 200-day are the most widely watched. Price above its 200-day average is commonly read as a sign the longer-term trend is up, below it the opposite. A "golden cross" (50-day crossing above the 200-day) and "death cross" (the reverse) are watched as longer-term trend-change signals, though both can lag the actual turn by weeks.
2. Support and resistance: price levels where a stock has repeatedly stopped falling or stopped rising in the past — the idea being that enough market participants remember those levels that they influence behavior again next time price approaches them. Neither is a hard floor or ceiling; both get broken regularly.
market_fundamentals.in_market_pulse: This is the SMA card and the momentum/trend classification on each stock's detail screen — computed directly from price history, not from an AI's read of a chart. The forward calls feature tracks how a classified setup (e.g. a momentum or mean-reversion read) actually played out over the following trading sessions — a historical record of the app's own calls, not a prediction of what comes next.
market_fundamentals.doesnt_tell_you: A crossing average or a broken level describes what price already did, not what it does next. Both signals lag the move they're named for, and a meaningful share of golden crosses and broken support levels fail to confirm the trend they seem to announce.

market_fundamentals.title: Support & Resistance
market_fundamentals.subtitle: Price levels the market keeps remembering, and why they tend to matter.
market_fundamentals.what_this_is: Price levels where buying or selling has repeatedly shown up — the idea being that enough market participants remember those levels that behavior tends to repeat near them. The 200-day SMA is the single most-watched support level on any major stock or index. "Holding" a level means price approached it and buyers stepped in. "Breaking" it means the level failed and the next one becomes relevant. Neither is permanent — levels get broken regularly.
market_fundamentals.key_ideas:
1. Support and resistance aren't exact prices — they're zones. Round numbers, prior highs and lows, and moving averages all attract this kind of memory effect, and different observers draw the zone slightly differently.
2. A broken resistance level often becomes support afterward, and vice versa — the same level, viewed from the other side.
3. The more times a level has been tested without breaking, the more significance the market tends to assign it if it finally does break.
market_fundamentals.in_market_pulse: The SMA Extension gauge shows how far SPY sits above or below its 200-day. The Key Levels section on each stock shows where recent support and resistance have formed from price history — computed from data, not drawn by hand.
market_fundamentals.doesnt_tell_you: A support level is a price where something happened before, not a guarantee it happens again.

market_fundamentals.title: Mean Reversion vs. Momentum
market_fundamentals.subtitle: Two opposing forces — trends that persist, and stretches that snap back.
market_fundamentals.what_this_is:
Two opposing forces in markets. Momentum says what's moving tends to keep moving — trending stocks attract more buyers, and trends can persist longer than expected. Mean reversion says extreme moves tend to snap back toward an average — a stock or index that has moved very far very fast has historically been more likely to pause or reverse than to keep accelerating at the same rate.

Neither is universally true. The regime matters: momentum strategies have worked better in trending macro environments; mean reversion has worked better in range-bound ones.
market_fundamentals.key_ideas:
1. RSI and SMA extension are the two most common ways to measure how "stretched" a move is — both feed a mean-reversion read, but a strong trend can hold both stretched for weeks without reverting.
2. Momentum tends to dominate mid-trend; mean reversion tends to dominate near exhaustion — but nothing here reliably tells you which phase you're in until after the fact.
3. A "Warning" classification isn't a reversal prediction — it flags that current behavior doesn't cleanly fit either pattern.
market_fundamentals.in_market_pulse: Every stock is classified as Momentum, Mean Reversion, Ranging, or Warning based on its current price behavior. Forward calls track how those classifications have resolved for that specific stock — the honest record of what happened next.
market_fundamentals.doesnt_tell_you: Which force is dominant right now. The classification names the current condition; the resolution is unknown.

market_fundamentals.title: Earnings Impact on Price
market_fundamentals.subtitle: Why a stock can fall on good news if expectations were even better.
market_fundamentals.what_this_is:
Markets are forward-looking — a stock's price reflects what investors expect about future earnings, not just current ones. This creates a "buy the rumor, sell the news" dynamic: if a company reports strong earnings but the result was already expected, the stock may not move — or may fall. What moves a stock is the gap between the reported number and what was expected ("the surprise").

Stocks often move in the days before an earnings report as traders position around expectations, and then sharply at the report itself.
market_fundamentals.key_ideas:
1. Guidance — a company's own forecast for the next quarter — often moves a stock more than the quarter that just ended, since the market is pricing what comes next, not what already happened.
2. A "beat" on earnings with a falling stock price usually means expectations, not the headline number, were what mattered.
3. The pre-report positioning traders take can unwind just as sharply as the reaction to the report itself, in either direction.
market_fundamentals.in_market_pulse: The fundamentals section shows the next earnings date and whether it's pre-market or after-close. The daily digest after a report summarizes the result and initial reaction.
market_fundamentals.doesnt_tell_you: How big the post-earnings move will be. Implied moves from options are one way the market prices that uncertainty — the app doesn't currently show this.

market_fundamentals.title: Sector Rotation
market_fundamentals.subtitle: Which sectors tend to lead and lag as the economic cycle shifts.
market_fundamentals.what_this_is:
As the economic cycle shifts, different sectors tend to lead and lag. Early expansion: cyclicals and financials. Late expansion: energy and materials. Slowdown: healthcare and staples. Recession: utilities and consumer staples. This isn't a rule — it's a tendency, and the cycle rarely follows a clean script.

The XLY/XLP ratio (Consumer Discretionary vs. Consumer Staples) is one of the cleanest real-time reads on which direction the rotation is leaning — are investors buying wants or needs?
market_fundamentals.key_ideas:
1. Rotation shows up first in relative performance, not absolute price — a sector can be rotating into leadership while still posting a loss, as long as it's losing less than the rest of the market.
2. The XLY/XLP ratio is a two-sector read; a fuller picture also weighs energy, financials, and defensives against each other, which the app doesn't combine into a single score.
3. A rotation signal and the broader cycle phase move together but not in lockstep — one can appear before, during, or well after the phase it's usually associated with.
market_fundamentals.in_market_pulse: Consumer Rotation in the Systemic Risk gauge tracks this directly. A ratio above 1.7 (Offensive) suggests risk appetite in consumer spending; below 1.25 (Flight to Safety) suggests defense.
market_fundamentals.doesnt_tell_you: Where in the cycle we are — that requires combining this signal with macro, credit, and earnings data.

market_fundamentals.title: Rate Sensitivity by Asset Class
market_fundamentals.subtitle: Why some assets flinch at rate changes far more than others.
market_fundamentals.what_this_is:
Not all stocks respond to rising rates the same way. Growth stocks (whose value depends heavily on future earnings) are mathematically more sensitive to rising rates — higher rates discount those future earnings more heavily, compressing their valuations. Value stocks, financials, and dividend payers tend to be less rate-sensitive or even rate-benefiting in some cases. Bonds fall in price when rates rise (a fixed coupon is worth less when new bonds pay more).

The Equity Risk Premium is the cleanest single measure of how rate moves are affecting the relative attractiveness of stocks vs. Treasuries — when it falls below 2%, bonds are offering nearly as much yield as equities, with less risk.
market_fundamentals.key_ideas:
1. Duration is the underlying concept: the longer it takes for an asset's cash flows to arrive, the more its present value moves when the discount rate changes. Long-duration growth stocks and long-maturity bonds sit at one end; short-duration value stocks and cash-like instruments sit at the other.
2. Financials are a partial exception — a steeper yield curve, not just a higher rate level, tends to help bank lending margins, which can offset some of the general rate-sensitivity pattern.
3. Rate sensitivity describes direction of impact, not size — two similarly "long duration" growth stocks can react very differently depending on their own balance sheets.
market_fundamentals.in_market_pulse: Fed Funds and the 10-year are in Macro Vitals (polarity inverted — rising = red). ERP is in the Valuation gauge.
market_fundamentals.doesnt_tell_you: Which specific stocks in your watchlist are most exposed — that requires knowing their earnings duration and leverage, which the app doesn't compute.

market_fundamentals.title: Breadth Divergence
market_fundamentals.subtitle: When an index rises but most of its own stocks don't.
market_fundamentals.what_this_is:
A market index can rise while most of its constituent stocks fall — if a handful of very large companies go up enough, they pull the cap-weighted index with them. This is breadth divergence: the index is up, but the average stock isn't. It's historically been read as a sign that a rally is becoming fragile — fewer stocks are participating, which means fewer buyers sustaining it.

The equal-weight vs. cap-weight comparison (RSP vs. SPY) makes this visible directly: if RSP is lagging SPY, the mega-caps are doing the work alone.
market_fundamentals.key_ideas:
1. Breadth divergence describes index composition, not company fundamentals — it shows how concentrated the gains are, not whether the leading companies deserve them.
2. Narrow breadth can persist through an entire bull-market leg — some of the longest rallies on record stayed breadth-narrow for extended stretches before broadening or breaking.
3. Widening breadth is generally read as healthier than narrowing, but a sudden widening after a long narrow stretch can also mark a rally's final stage rather than its start.
market_fundamentals.in_market_pulse: Market Breadth tracks the 1-day change in RSP/SPY. A sustained Narrowing reading (RSP consistently lagging) is more meaningful than a single day.
market_fundamentals.doesnt_tell_you: How long a narrow rally can persist — it can go on for months. Breadth is a condition, not a timer.

tactical_momentum.subtitle: Short-term sentiment and momentum — how fast the market's moving, and how nervous it is.
tactical_momentum.what_this_is: Tactical Momentum measures the short-term pulse of market sentiment and price momentum — how fast things are moving, and whether investors are fearful or complacent.
tactical_momentum.the_signals:
1. Fear & Greed (CNN) — composite market mood, 0–100
2. Put/Call Ratio — how defensively options traders are positioned
3. SPY RSI 14-day — speed and size of recent price moves
4. SMA Extension 200-day — how far SPY sits above/below its long-term trend
5. VIX — expected 30-day market volatility
tactical_momentum.how_to_read_together:
These five signals are most useful when they agree. RSI overbought (>70) alongside low Put/Call (<0.6) and calm VIX (<20) describes a complacent market with little hedging — a different picture than RSI overbought with VIX spiking above 30 (fear entering a stretched market, which tends to resolve more sharply).

Agreement across signals is a stronger read than any single gauge.
tactical_momentum.what_to_watch:
1. Whether Fear & Greed sustains an extreme (>75 or <25) across multiple days — brief touches mean less than a stretch
2. SMA Extension crossing +10%: price is running well ahead of its 200-day trend line
3. VIX moving from calm (<20) to elevated (>20) while RSI is still high — the combination that has historically preceded sharper pullbacks
tactical_momentum.common_misreads: RSI above 70 is a condition, not a sell signal — strong trends can stay overbought for weeks. Fear & Greed at an extreme doesn't mean a reversal is imminent; it means the crowd is leaning hard one way. VIX measures expected volatility, not direction — a high VIX says movement is expected, not which way it goes.
tactical_momentum.in_the_wild:
Scenario: Fear & Greed at 81, Put/Call at 0.55, VIX at 14, RSI at 74, SMA Extension at +12%.

All five pointing the same direction — elevated risk appetite, low hedging, price stretched above trend. Historically this kind of broad agreement has marked periods where the market was pricing in a lot of good news already. Whether that matters for what you're watching is yours to judge.

systemic_risk.subtitle: Credit, volatility, currency, and breadth — the stress signals underneath price.
systemic_risk.what_this_is: Systemic Risk tracks the structural stress signals beneath price — credit markets, volatility in bonds, currency strength, commodity signals, and whether the rally has broad participation.
systemic_risk.the_signals:
1. Yield Curve (10Y−2Y) — gap between long and short Treasury rates
2. Credit Spreads — extra yield demanded for risky corporate bonds
3. MOVE Index — bond-market volatility
4. Copper/Gold Ratio — growth appetite vs. safety demand
5. Consumer Rotation (XLY/XLP) — risk appetite in spending behavior
6. Market Breadth (RSP/SPY) — equal vs. cap-weight S&P performance
7. US Dollar (DXY) — dollar strength, global conditions proxy
8. Crude Oil — inflation/demand signal
systemic_risk.how_to_read_together:
Systemic risk tends to show up in credit and bonds before it shows in stocks. Widening credit spreads (>3.0%), elevated MOVE (>100), and an inverted yield curve together describe a market where professionals are already pricing in stress — even when the stock price level hasn't moved yet.

Breadth adds another layer: a narrow market (RSP lagging SPY) alongside rising credit spreads means the stress is visible in multiple dimensions simultaneously. The Copper/Gold ratio and Consumer Rotation confirm whether the broader economy is leaning toward growth or defense.
systemic_risk.what_to_watch:
1. The yield curve crossing zero (inversion) — historically the most watched recession warning
2. Credit spreads moving above 3.0% (Caution) or 4.0% (Stress) — the bond market repricing default risk
3. Breadth narrowing (RSP consistently lagging SPY) while indices are flat or rising — a rally carried by fewer and fewer stocks
systemic_risk.common_misreads: An inverted yield curve predicts a slowdown, not its timing — the gap between inversion and any economic impact has varied from months to over a year. The Copper/Gold and Consumer Rotation ratios are this app's own composite lenses, not named Wall Street indicators — treat them as directional, not precise. A strong dollar is a headwind, not a verdict.
systemic_risk.in_the_wild:
Scenario: yield curve at −0.4% (Inverted), credit spreads at 3.8% (approaching Stress), MOVE at 115 (Elevated), breadth Narrowing.

Four different signals from different parts of the market pointing toward stress simultaneously. None guarantees an outcome — but when credit, rates, volatility, and breadth all move the same direction, the market is pricing in something. What you make of it is yours.

valuation.subtitle: Is the market cheap or expensive, and compared to what.
valuation.what_this_is: Valuation asks whether the price being paid for the market is reasonable relative to what it earns, owns, and yields — and compared to the alternative of holding risk-free Treasuries.
valuation.the_signals:
1. P/E Ratio (TTM) — price per dollar of trailing earnings
2. Price-to-Book — price relative to net asset value
3. Equity Risk Premium — earnings yield vs. the 10-year Treasury
4. Dividend Yield — income return on the index
valuation.how_to_read_together:
These four measures tell the same story from different angles — read them for agreement, not individually. A high P/E alongside a low dividend yield and a shrinking ERP (below 2.0%) describes a market where equities offer little premium over Treasuries and price a lot of future growth already. When P/B also sits in Premium territory (>4.5x), all four are confirming the same "richly priced" read.

The ERP is the most useful single number here — it anchors valuation to the real alternative (Treasuries) rather than to history alone.
valuation.what_to_watch:
1. ERP falling below 2.0% — the Dangerous zone where equities offer very little premium over the risk-free rate
2. P/E above 22 alongside rising 10-year yields — multiple compression risk (valuations come under pressure when rates rise)
3. All four gauges in their stretched zones simultaneously — rare, but a strong read when it happens
valuation.common_misreads: A low P/E is not automatically cheap — it frequently means the market has already priced in a real concern. Valuation tells you what's priced in; it says nothing about when or whether price corrects. These are SPY-level figures, not individual stock valuations. The P/B and dividend yield are blunter tools for a modern index than historically (much S&P value is now intangible).
valuation.in_the_wild:
Scenario: P/E at 24 (Expensive), ERP at 1.6% (Dangerous), dividend yield at 1.3% (Low), 10-year yield rising.

All four pointing rich — and rates rising means the ERP is compressing further in real time. This describes a market pricing in significant future earnings growth with little margin of safety versus Treasuries. What you conclude from that picture is yours.

macro_vitals.subtitle: Inflation, jobs, growth, and rates — the numbers that drive the Fed's next move.
macro_vitals.what_this_is: Macro Vitals tracks the economy's underlying health — inflation, jobs, growth, and the policy rate that sits above all of it. These are the numbers that drive what the Fed does next, which in turn drives everything else.
macro_vitals.the_signals:
1. CPI YoY — headline inflation vs. a year ago
2. Core PCE YoY + MoM — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, annual + monthly
3. Unemployment Rate — jobless rate trend
4. Nonfarm Payrolls — monthly net jobs added/lost
5. Real GDP — inflation-adjusted economic growth (quarterly)
6. Retail Sales MoM — consumer spending pulse
7. Federal Funds Rate — the Fed's policy lever (polarity inverted: rising = red)
8. 10-Year Treasury Yield — market-set benchmark rate (polarity inverted)
macro_vitals.how_to_read_together:
The macro picture is a sequence, not a snapshot. Start with inflation (CPI + core PCE) — it sets what the Fed is likely to do. Then jobs (unemployment + payrolls) — a strong labor market lets the Fed stay tighter longer; a weakening one raises the odds of cuts. GDP and retail sales confirm whether the real economy is absorbing the rate environment.

The 10-year yield is the market's real-time vote on where all of this is heading — it moves before the Fed does. Watch for divergence: if payrolls are strong but retail sales are falling, the consumer may be weakening before it shows in job numbers.
macro_vitals.what_to_watch:
1. Core PCE MoM accelerating while YoY is still falling — the monthly rate turns before the annual one, earliest inflation signal
2. Unemployment rising from a low base — even a 0.3–0.5% move off a trough has historically been an early slowdown tell
3. 10-year yield moving in the opposite direction to Fed Funds — the market pricing a policy shift before it happens
macro_vitals.common_misreads: These are monthly and quarterly figures — a flat line in the app is the release cadence, not stale data. GDP is quarterly; payrolls and CPI are monthly; the 10-year moves continuously. The Fed Funds and 10-year yield colors are polarity-inverted: red means rising (more restrictive), green means falling — don't read the color as "the number went down." One strong payrolls print doesn't reverse a trend.
macro_vitals.in_the_wild:
Scenario: Core PCE MoM reaccelerating (Hot), unemployment ticking up two months in a row, 10-year yield falling while Fed Funds holds flat.

Inflation reaccelerating while the labor market softens and the bond market starts pricing cuts — three signals pointing in different directions. The market is betting the Fed pivots before inflation is fully solved. Whether that bet is right is the question worth watching.

posture.subtitle: What professional money is actually doing beneath the surface of price.
posture.what_this_is: Posture reads how professional and institutional money is positioned beneath the surface of price — not what the market is doing, but what the people running large pools of capital are doing about it.
posture.the_signals:
1. NAAIM Exposure Index — active fund managers' actual equity exposure
2. Dark Pool Index (DIX) — buy-side share of institutional off-exchange volume
3. Net Liquidity (Fed balance sheet − TGA − Reverse Repo) — system-wide cash
posture.how_to_read_together:
Posture is deliberately not price-based — that's what makes it useful. The most informative read is divergence: when NAAIM is low (managers defensively positioned) but DIX is rising (institutions quietly buying off-exchange), the surface narrative and the actual behavior are pointing in different directions.

Net Liquidity provides the macro plumbing context — expanding liquidity has historically been a tailwind for risk assets regardless of sentiment. All three agreeing (managers cautious + DIX accumulating + liquidity expanding) describes a setup where the professional positioning backstory is more constructive than the headlines.
posture.what_to_watch:
1. NAAIM below 40 (Extreme Fear/Hedged) with DIX above 45 (Accumulation) — the clearest manager-vs-institutional divergence signal
2. Net Liquidity direction flipping from Expanding to Draining — a slow-moving signal but meaningful when it persists
3. NAAIM above 100 (leveraged long) — managers have no dry powder left to push higher from here
posture.common_misreads: NAAIM is a weekly survey with a lag — it describes positioning as of last week, not today. Net Liquidity classifies by direction with no dead-band — a tiny move still reads Expanding or Draining, so a single flip means less than a sustained trend. DIX accumulation doesn't mean institutions are right; it means they're buying. The band cutoffs on all three are this app's own (not-backtested) — treat them as directional, not precise thresholds.
posture.in_the_wild:
Scenario: NAAIM at 38 (Extreme Fear), DIX at 47 (Accumulation), Net Liquidity Expanding.

Active managers are heavily hedged while dark-pool institutional buying is elevated and system liquidity is growing. Three signals pointing toward a constructive backstory beneath a fearful surface. Whether that divergence resolves the way it has historically is the question — the app shows you the gap; the conclusion is yours.

positioning.subtitle: Where retail, futures speculators, and short sellers each stand — and whether they agree.
positioning.what_this_is:
Positioning tracks where three distinct crowds stand — retail investors, large futures speculators, and short sellers — each on their own timescale. The value is in seeing where they agree or diverge.

Note: this is different from the "positioning" metric in Indicators (which tracks SPY's 52-week range). Same word, different data.
positioning.the_signals:
1. AAII Bull-Bear Spread — weekly retail investor sentiment survey
2. CFTC COT Net %OI + Percentile — large speculator futures positioning (S&P, Nasdaq, Russell), raw and vs. recent history
3. FINRA Short Interest — shares sold short, days to cover, MoM change
positioning.how_to_read_together:
The three crowds move on different timescales and with different motivations — retail (AAII) is weekly and emotional, futures speculators (COT) are professional and leveraged, short sellers (FINRA) are committing capital to a specific directional bet.

The most informative reads are extremes and divergences: retail at peak bearishness (read contrarian) while the COT percentile shows speculator longs near historic highs describes two crowds pulling in opposite directions. When all three are crowded the same way, the risk of an unwind grows — a crowded trade is a fragile one.
positioning.what_to_watch:
1. AAII at an extreme (very high bullish or very bearish spread) — historically a contrarian signal, though it can persist
2. COT percentile above 80 or below 20 — speculator positioning at an extreme relative to its own recent history
3. Short interest days-to-cover rising while price is also rising — potential squeeze setup building
positioning.common_misreads: AAII is famously unreliable as a timing tool — extreme readings have preceded reversals, but the lag varies enormously. COT data is released Friday for Tuesday's positions — it's inherently lagged. FINRA short interest is twice-monthly; treat it as a slow-moving backdrop, not a real-time read. The app reports raw short shares and month-over-month change, not short-%-of-float (that data isn't available from this source).
positioning.in_the_wild:
Scenario: AAII spread at −35% (very bearish retail), COT percentile at 22 (speculators near historically light longs), short interest days-to-cover rising.

All three crowds leaning the same direction — defensively. Historically, this kind of broad crowd agreement on the bearish side has been a contrarian data point worth noting. Whether it is here is yours to judge.

stock_analysis.subtitle: Price trend, setup, valuation, and macro context for one stock, synthesized into plain language.
stock_analysis.what_this_is: Stock Analysis synthesizes price trend, technical setup, valuation, and macro context for individual stocks into a plain-language read updated after each trading session and a deeper dive every two weeks.
stock_analysis.the_signals:
1. Setup classification (Momentum / Mean Reversion / Ranging / Warning)
2. SMA trend (50-day and 200-day relative to price)
3. Key levels (support/resistance from recent price history)
4. Valuation (P/E vs. sector median — sector-relative, not market-wide)
5. Macro alignment (whether the stock's setup aligns with the macro regime)
6. Forward calls (how previous setups actually resolved over 5 sessions)
7. Daily digest (end-of-day AI summary, news + price action)
8. Deep dive (biweekly extended analysis across trend, valuation, scenarios)
stock_analysis.how_to_read_together:
Start with the setup classification — it frames everything else. A Momentum setup in a risk-on macro regime, with price above both moving averages and sector-relative P/E not at an extreme, is a coherent picture. The same Momentum setup in a risk-off regime with stretched valuation introduces tension — the setup and the backdrop are pulling in different directions.

Key levels give you the specific price context; forward calls give you the honest record of how similar setups have resolved in this stock before.
stock_analysis.what_to_watch:
1. Whether the setup classification and the macro regime agree or conflict — alignment is cleaner; conflict raises the question of which one is right
2. How previous forward calls resolved — a stock with a strong completion rate on Momentum calls is a different proposition than one where those calls have historically faded
3. Sector-relative P/E diverging sharply from the absolute P/E — the stock can look cheap vs. the market and expensive vs. its peers
stock_analysis.common_misreads: The setup classification names a condition in price behavior — it is not a prediction of what comes next. "Momentum" means the stock has been trending; it says nothing about whether the trend continues. The deep dive is AI-written from the available data — it can miss context, misread a conflicting signal, or overstate confidence. Cross-check anything in the deep dive against the underlying numbers on the same screen.
stock_analysis.in_the_wild:
Scenario: a stock classified Momentum, price above both SMAs, P/E 10% below sector median, macro regime risk-on, last three forward calls all completed positive.

All the signals a Momentum read would want to see are present. The forward-call history shows this specific stock has followed through before in similar conditions. Whether it does again is the question — the app shows you the setup, the conclusion is yours.

cards.title: How to read any gauge
cards.body: Every gauge in Market Pulse turns a raw number into a colored reading through the same three steps — knowing them makes any gauge legible.

cards.title: The three steps
cards.body:
1. The raw value — a real measured number: an index level, a ratio, a yield, a percent. This is data, computed in code. The AI never sets it.

2. The band — the app sorts that raw value into a labeled zone (e.g. "Overbought," "Inverted," "Extreme Greed") using fixed cutoffs. These cutoffs are written into the code, not decided per-run. Some are standard market conventions (RSI ≥ 70 = overbought); others are the app's own reasonable lines (P/E ≥ 22 = expensive) — the glossary tells you which is which.

3. The color — the band maps to green / amber / red as a quick visual cue. Green is not "buy" and red is not "sell" — they mark where a reading sits on its own scale, nothing more. A red "Restrictive" on the Fed Funds rate just means rates are rising; whether that's good or bad for a given stock is yours to judge.

cards.title: Three things worth knowing
cards.body:
1. Not every gauge reads its raw level: Market Breadth, Net Liquidity, and several macro gauges (payrolls, retail sales, Fed Funds, the 10-year) are classified by their direction of change instead. "Expanding" or "Rising" means the number moved that way recently — a different question than whether it's high or low.
2. A couple are polarity-inverted: for the Fed Funds rate and the 10-year yield, a rising number shows red ("Restrictive") and a falling one green, because higher rates tighten conditions. Don't read the color as "the number went down."
3. Some gauges have no color at all on certain fields (raw share counts, for instance) — those are pure data with no band, shown as a number to read directly.

The gauge names the condition. What it means for your decisions is the part only you can supply.

cards.title: Two words this app uses twice
cards.body:
"Positioning" — Market Pulse uses this word for two unrelated things. On the Insights → Positioning tab, it means how three crowds are leaning (retail sentiment, futures speculators, short sellers). As an Indicators metric, "positioning" refers to where SPY sits in its 52-week range. Same word, different data, no relationship between them.

"Market regime" — One is a deterministic, code-computed label (risk-on / risk-off / neutral) built from trend, breadth, volatility, and rates. The other is a phrase the AI Macro Hub may use in its own written verdict. The code-computed one is the app's factual classification; the AI one is narrative. They can differ, and that's expected.

cards.title: A Few Things Worth Knowing About the Data Itself
cards.body:
1. Market holidays and half-days: some indicators may show a stale "last close" value rather than a fresh one.
2. After-hours vs. regular-hours pricing: a price shown outside market hours may reflect after-hours trading, which is typically lower-volume and more volatile than regular-hours pricing.
3. Halted or delisted symbols: data for a halted or delisted symbol may be missing or frozen at its last known value.
4. Delayed data: most market data is not real-time; treat displayed prices as approximate, not tradeable quotes.
